content: 1. Imaging studies have demonstrated that engaging in activities such as music, exercise, or meditation can lead to enduring changes in brain structure, function, or both. 2. This evidence underscores the principle that repeated, activity-dependent experiences can have a lasting impact on the brain. 3. Research suggests that reinforcing specific oscillatory patterns through EEG neurofeedback training increases the likelihood of these patterns being more easily reproduced in the future. 4. For example, the beta rhythm effect is robust enough to be detectable even three years after EEG neurofeedback training. 5. This finding supports the foundational premise of EEG neurofeedback: the brain can be conditioned to exhibit specific oscillatory patterns. 6. Theoretically, this phenomenon may be explained by a combination of established plasticity mechanisms, such as associative and homeostatic forms. 7. Associative (Hebbian) plasticity posits that synapses that fire together, wire together, and synapses that fire apart, wire apart. 8. Neurophysiological evidence indicates that the amplitude of EEG oscillations is enhanced by the number of neurons or synaptic potentials involved. 9. With repeated training, the connections between neuron populations that are amplified or synchronized to create a specific oscillatory pattern are strengthened, facilitating the future generation of this pattern. 10. A common hypothesis across these theories is that neural circuitry can be modified, likely resulting in observable behavioral changes. 11. During EEG neurofeedback, electrodes placed on the scalp measure the synchronized, rhythmic fluctuations of local field potentials from groups of neurons, known as neural oscillations. 12. These oscillations arise from the excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) of large groups of neurons, producing a measurable EEG signal at the scalp level. 13. Synchronized oscillatory activities are associated with cognitive abilities such as inhibition, updating of working memory, and temporary maintenance of information in working memory, suggesting that neural oscillations are a fundamental functional mechanism in cortical computation. 14. Executive functions are critical for daily life, mediating the performance of complex tasks, academic achievement, and long-term success. 15. EEG neurofeedback treatment offers potential for preventing and addressing executive functioning difficulties in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. 16. New EEG neurofeedback protocols are continually being tested to determine their effectiveness in reducing or remediating executive functioning difficulties, such as inhibition and updating, in neurodevelopmental disorders. 17. However, the commercial use of EEG neurofeedback currently outpaces the evidence base supporting its efficacy. 18. The economic cost of this intervention is high for parents, and patient desperation is also significant. 19. A history of poorly researched interventions for children has prompted the professional community to prioritize accountability in establishing the effectiveness of new treatments as a matter of professional ethics. 20. The use of EEG neurofeedback as an intervention for children with neurodevelopmental problems has reached a critical juncture, necessitating rigorous evaluation of its evidence base. 21. This systematic review is the first of its kind and will make a unique contribution to the EEG neurofeedback literature. 22. It serves as a preliminary step for further investigations into the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of this intervention. 23. If the effectiveness of EEG neurofeedback is supported by this review, additional research may explore its applicability to other mental health conditions or age groups. 24. Neurodevelopmental disorders affect a significant proportion of the population, including conditions such as autism, ADHD, and intellectual disabilities. 25. Autism is estimated to affect 1 in 160 children worldwide, equating to over 7.6 million disability-adjusted life years and 0.3% of the global disease burden. 26. ADHD affects an estimated 39 million people globally. In the United States, approximately 11% of children aged 4 to 17 years (6.4 million) are affected. 27. In Australia, 7.4% (298,000) of children aged 4 to 17 years with a mental disorder between 2013 and 2014 were diagnosed with ADHD. 28. Among children aged 5 to 14 years, ADHD accounts for an estimated 3.4% of total years lived in ill health or with disability, making it the eighth leading cause of non-fatal health loss in this age group in Australia. 29. Intellectual disabilities affect an average of 10.37 individuals per 1,000 people globally, according to an international meta-analysis across 29 countries. 30. In Australia, intellectual disabilities are the seventh leading cause of non-fatal health loss for children aged birth to five years, accounting for an estimated 4.3% of total years lived in ill health or with disability. 31. Down syndrome, fetal alcohol spectrum (FAS) disorder, and fragile X syndrome have received limited attention in statistical accounts, resulting in limited epidemiological data on these specific intellectual disorders. 32. The incidence rate for Down syndrome is estimated to be around 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,100 live births worldwide. 33. In Western Australia, the estimated prevalence of FAS disorder was 0.4 per 1,000 live births between 2000 and 2004. 34. Between 1990 and 2005, the reported prevalence of FAS disorder in Canada, Italy, and the United States ranged from 30.52 to 47.13 per 1,000, while in South Africa, the prevalence was particularly high at 113.22 per 1,000. 35. In the absence of life expectancy data for fragile X syndrome, prevalence rates are expected to remain consistent across all age groups due to the strong genetic component of this disorder. 36. In Australia, the number of individuals with fragile X syndrome is estimated to range from 1,362 to 4,309 for those with a full mutation and intellectual disability, and from 13,466 to 87,137 for those with a premutation. 37. In Europe, 1 in 3,717 individuals of European descent is estimated to be affected by fragile X syndrome. 38. In the United Kingdom, 1 in 5,530 individuals is projected to receive a diagnosis of fragile X syndrome, while in the United States, the condition is anticipated to occur in 1 in 5,161 males. 39. Neurodevelopmental disorders impose a significant burden on individuals, families, and communities. 40. Understanding causal pathways with the aim of prevention or remediation should be considered a priority.
